Simulate range shifts with dispersal and colonisation-extinction dynamics

geo_shift_simulate.Rd

geo_shift_simulate() projects where a species can actually be, not only where the climate suits it. Correlative niche models assume that a species fills all suitable habitat at once; real species colonise new habitat at the speed of their dispersal and lose populations where conditions deteriorate, often with a lag. This function runs a spatially explicit, stochastic colonisation-extinction model (a stochastic patch occupancy model on a grid; Hanski 1999; Engler and Guisan 2009) over a time series of habitat suitability, such as the output of a species distribution model projected onto successive climate periods.

In each step, an empty cell \(j\) is colonised with probability $$1 - \exp(-c \, s_j \sum_i K(d_{ij})),$$ where the sum runs over occupied cells \(i\) and \(K\) is the dispersal kernel, truncated at max_distance and normalised to sum to 1 over the neighbourhood (so the sum is the kernel-weighted share of occupied neighbours, and results do not depend on the cell size). Two kernels are offered, both parameterised by their mean dispersal distance \(\bar d\) in two dimensions:

  • "exponential": \(K(d) \propto e^{-2d/\bar d}\);

  • "2Dt" (Clark et al. 1999): \(K(d) \propto (1 + d^2/u)^{-(p+1)}\), fat-tailed, so rare long-distance dispersal is far more likely than under the exponential; smaller kernel_shape (\(p > 0.5\)) gives a fatter tail. Use geo_dispersal_kernel() to see a kernel's realised mean and tail.

Optional processes:

  • resistance: movement costs. The distance is replaced by an effective distance, the straight-line distance times the mean resistance of the cells crossed (1 = baseline, 5 = five times harder, below 1 = corridor; NA, 0 or Inf = impassable barrier). This is a local, straight-line approximation, not a least-cost path.

  • jump_rate and jump_weights: human-assisted or other long-distance jumps. Each step, a Poisson number of propagules with mean jump_rate times the number of occupied cells lands on cells chosen in proportion to jump_weights (for example road density, ports or towns), and establishes with probability equal to suitability.

  • disturbance: the probability, per step, that an occupied cell is lost to clearing, fire or eradication, on top of the climate.

\(s_j\) is the suitability of the cell and \(c\) the colonisation rate. An occupied cell persists with probability \(s_j^p\). Cell sizes come from the grid's true geometry, so the kernel is isotropic in metres on longitude/latitude grids. Simulations run in parallel in C++ with independent random streams; results depend on seed but not on the number of threads.

The result is the probability that each cell is occupied at the end of each period, over nsim simulations. Compare it with the suitability itself (unlimited dispersal) to see the dispersal lag, the extinction debt and whether a species can cross gaps in habitat.

Usage

geo_shift_simulate(
  suitability,
  initial = 0.5,
  dispersal_mean,
  max_distance = NULL,
  colonisation = 1,
  persistence = 1,
  steps_per_layer = 1,
  nsim = 100,
  seed = NULL,
  threads = 0,
  kernel = c("exponential", "2Dt"),
  kernel_shape = 1,
  resistance = NULL,
  jump_rate = 0,
  jump_weights = NULL,
  disturbance = NULL
)

geo_shift_summary(occupancy, elevation = NULL)

Arguments

suitability

A SpatRaster with one layer per time period (values 0 to 1; NA or negative values are unsuitable, e.g. sea).

initial

Starting occupancy: a SpatRaster (cells > 0 occupied), an sf table of occurrence points, or a number, the suitability threshold applied to the first layer.

dispersal_mean

Mean dispersal distance per step, in metres.

max_distance

Largest dispersal distance in metres (kernel truncation); default five times the mean for the exponential kernel and ten times for the 2Dt kernel.

colonisation

Colonisation rate \(c\).

persistence

Exponent \(p\) of local persistence; larger values make populations in marginal habitat more likely to disappear.

steps_per_layer

Number of dispersal generations within each period (for example 10 for ten-year periods and a species that disperses once a year).

nsim

Number of stochastic simulations.

seed

Random seed.

threads

Number of threads (0 = OpenMP default).

kernel

"exponential" or "2Dt" (fat-tailed).

kernel_shape

Shape \(p\) of the 2Dt kernel (above 0.5; smaller is fatter-tailed).

resistance

Optional SpatRaster of movement resistance (1 = baseline; NA, 0 or Inf = barrier).

jump_rate

Expected number of long-distance jumps per occupied cell per step (default 0, none).

jump_weights

Optional SpatRaster of relative weights of jump destinations; default all cells equally.

disturbance

Optional SpatRaster of the probability that an occupied cell is lost per step: one layer, or one per layer of suitability.

occupancy

Result of geo_shift_simulate() (or a suitability raster, for comparison).

elevation

Optional elevation SpatRaster on the same grid; adds the occupancy-weighted 5%, 50% and 95% elevations (lower edge, centre and upper edge).

Value

geo_shift_simulate(): a SpatRaster of occupancy probability, one layer per period, named after the layers of suitability, with the settings as attribute "settings".

geo_shift_summary(): a tibble with one row per period: period, area_km2 (expected occupied area), and with elevation, lower, median and upper.

References

Engler, R. and Guisan, A. (2009). MigClim: predicting plant distribution and dispersal in a changing climate. Diversity and Distributions, 15, 590-601.

Hanski, I. (1999). Metapopulation Ecology. Oxford University Press.

Clark, J. S., Silman, M., Kern, R., Macklin, E. and HilleRisLambers, J. (1999). Seed dispersal near and far: patterns across temperate and tropical forests. Ecology, 80, 1475-1494.

See also

geo_dispersal_kernel(), geo_epidemic_simulate(), geo_shift_summary(), sdm_ensemble(), geo_range_shift().

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("terra", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # A virtual mountain: suitability is a band that moves upslope
  r <- terra::rast(
    nrows = 40, ncols = 40, xmin = 145, xmax = 145.4,
    ymin = -6.4, ymax = -6, crs = "EPSG:4326"
  )
  elev <- terra::init(r, "y")
  elev <- (elev - min(terra::values(elev))) * 10000
  band <- function(mid) exp(-((elev - mid) / 400)^2)
  suit <- c(band(1000), band(1400), band(1800))
  names(suit) <- c("2000", "2050", "2100")
  occ <- geo_shift_simulate(suit, 0.5, dispersal_mean = 2000, nsim = 20, seed = 1)
  geo_shift_summary(occ, elevation = elev)
}
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   period area_km2 lower median upper
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 2000      290.   700.  1000. 1300.
#> 2 2050      158.   900.  1200. 1500.
#> 3 2100       46.2 1100.  1400. 1700 
# }
